eb565a991b544039: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah
For most of my life, I have described myself, rather cheerfully, as a Jill of all trades and master of none.
I have tried my hand at almost everything.

I cook. I sew. I embroider. I design. I garden. I collect. I write. I make things. I take things apart and put them together again. I become fascinated by something, pursue it with enormous enthusiasm, and before long, another curiosity comes knocking at the door.
My hands have never been very good at keeping still, and neither, I suspect, has my mind.
But there was always one thing I never really thought of myself as being.
A scholar.
That belonged to another world: to academics, professors, historians and people who seemed to have known from a very young age exactly what they wanted to study and what they wanted to become.
I was already 64 when I returned seriously to academic life.
At an age when one is perhaps expected to slow down, I did precisely the opposite.
I went back to school.
And somewhere between lectures, books, manuscripts, footnotes and many very late nights, something quite unexpected happened.
I fell in love with learning.
Not with examinations. Not with grades. Not even with the idea of obtaining a degree.
I fell in love with the chase.

One question led to another. One footnote opened another door. A sentence written hundreds of years ago could keep me awake at night. I began looking at old manuscripts and wondering who had held them, who had written them, why certain words had been chosen, and what they might tell us that history had forgotten.
Then I met the Hukum Kanun Pahang.
Or perhaps, more accurately, I met it again.
It had been there all along. But for the first time, I began to see it not merely as an old manuscript belonging to Pahang, but as a voice from another age.
And I began asking questions.
Too many questions, according to some people around me.

One discovery became another. Melaka led me to Pahang. Pahang led me to Sultan Abdul Ghaffar Muhyiddin Shah. The laws led me to the sea. The sea led me to sovereignty. And somewhere along the way, the thesis I thought I was going to write began refusing to become the thesis I had planned.
That was perhaps my first real lesson as a student.
Do not tell history what you want it to say.
Listen to what the evidence is trying to tell you.
So I followed it.

I followed it through manuscripts and histories, through laws and royal genealogies, through ports and rivers, through Melaka and Pahang, sometimes with excitement, sometimes with frustration, and occasionally with tears.
And on July 27, at the age of 65, I submitted my Master’s thesis:
The Hukum Kanun Pahang: A Sovereign Malay-Islamic Constitution.
A few weeks later, I received my examination results.
The average mark from the two examiners was 91%.
My internal examiner recommended the thesis for acceptance without any modifications or amendments in content, while my external examiner required only very minor corrections.
I read the reports.
And then I cried.
I cried, and I screamed.
Not very scholarly behaviour, perhaps, but after months of work, doubt, discovery, late nights and wondering whether I had understood the manuscript correctly, I could not help myself.
I had never expected this.
But it was not only the marks, or even the absence of corrections from one examiner and the very minor corrections from the other, that moved me.
Both examiners believed that the work should go beyond the examination room.

My internal examiner wrote that the thesis demonstrated “originality, coherence, and scholarly adequacy” and was therefore “suitable for publication.” Its strength, he observed, lay in reframing the Hukum Kanun Pahang as a sovereign Malay-Islamic constitution, embedding Sharīʿah principles within adat, and highlighting the balance between royal authority and accountability.
He concluded that these contributions provided “a fresh civilisational lens that enriches Malay legal historiography.”

My external examiner similarly recommended that the findings of the thesis should be disseminated through academic publications and conference presentations, to highlight their importance to Malaysia’s inherited constitutional and legal identity.
Those words meant a great deal to me.

I had begun this journey simply wanting to understand an old manuscript that had captured my imagination. I never imagined that at the end of it, my examiners would tell me that what I had discovered deserved to travel beyond my thesis and into the wider academic world.
And then I laughed.
Because after spending most of my life calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none, at 66 years old I had finally managed to become—
a Master of one.
But perhaps that is not really what this story is about.
It is not about 91%.
It is not even about a Master’s degree.
It is about discovering, rather late in life, that curiosity has no retirement age.

We are very fond of putting ages upon things. There is an age to study, an age to marry, an age to raise children, an age to build a career and, apparently, an age when we should begin quietly withdrawing from new adventures.
I am beginning to think that is nonsense.
Some flowers bloom in spring.
Others take their time.

Perhaps being a late bloomer does not mean that one has arrived late. Perhaps all those earlier years, the cooking, sewing, creating, reading, raising children, serving, listening, observing, succeeding, failing, beginning again, were not detours at all.
Perhaps they were preparation.
Because when I finally entered that library and opened those manuscripts, I did not arrive there only as a student.
I brought a lifetime with me.
And perhaps that was my advantage.
I had spent 66 years learning before I realised that I was a learner.
I had spent a lifetime searching before I discovered what I was searching for.
I had spent years calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none.
Then, very late in the garden, a little flower appeared.
And I discovered that I had been growing all along.
I am a late bloomer.
And I think I rather like blooming late.
But above all, I know that all knowledge comes from Allah. Whatever I have learned, whatever I have discovered, and whatever little contribution I may have made are only by His permission and grace.
Alhamdulillah.

I thank Allah for giving me the opportunity, the strength and the curiosity to continue learning at this stage of my life. I pray that whatever knowledge He has entrusted to me may be used well, shared generously and become something of benefit to others.
I have just registered for my PhD.
And somewhere in the fifteenth century, Parameswara is waiting for me.

P/S: My husband insists that I clarify one important point: I met him before I met Hukum Kanun Pahang. So, in the interests of historical accuracy, let the record show that he was my first great discovery.

The Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah, holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia.
bcd44a93e77f0903: From Moaz Nair

For 69 years since the nation achieved independence, the non-Muslim community has been a significant strategic partner in the construction and development phases of Malaysia’s geopolitical landscape, spanning from the pre-independence era to the postmodern phase. Their roles extend across multiple critical domains that form the foundation of national identity and national stability.

However, contemporary political dynamics are occasionally still marred by the exploitation of religious and racial issues for narrow geopolitical interests, risking damage to the nation's social fabric.

An objective evaluation of the sacrifices made by non-Muslim communities is highly essential to appreciate their role as one of the main pillars in defending, advancing, and uniting the socioeconomic and political landscape of the country.
The struggle for independence

During the struggle for independence, non-Muslims demonstrated high political tolerance to establish a national consensus. Tan Cheng Lock and VT Sambanthan's participation in a delegation to London alongside Tunku Abdul Rahman reflected a unified goal in demanding independence for the Federation of Malaya.
Tan's role as the founder and first president of MCA in 1949 was highly instrumental as a political architect of unity.

When the Chinese community's loyalty was questioned during the Emergency, Tan united and convinced the community to pledge full commitment to the Federation of Malaya, rejecting the influence of communist ideology and the geopolitics of the People's Republic of China.

Substantive negotiations with Umno and a readiness to compromise and drop certain radical demands enabled the formation of the Social Contract. This legal and social instrument granted citizenship rights to non-Malays in exchange for the recognition of the special position of the Malays.
This pattern of cooperation was further reinforced by MIC within the Alliance Party.

The coalition, comprising Umno-MCA-MIC, demanded great political sacrifice to meet the prerequisites for independence set by the British. Post-1957, this legacy of inclusive governance continued through the active involvement of non-Muslim figures in the country’s executive and legislative institutions as ministers, members of Parliament, and senators.
Defence and security

In domestic defence and security, thousands of non-Muslim security personnel, including the indigenous communities from Sabah and Sarawak such as the Iban, Kadazan, and Bidayuh, were directly involved on the front lines to curb the communist insurgency threat.

Figures such as the late Warrant Officer I Temenggong Kanang anak Langkau, recipient of the prestigious Seri Pahlawan Gagah Perkasa (SPG) gallantry award, became the epitome of the national resilience doctrine.

His commitment was proven by his refusal to surrender despite sustaining severe injuries from three gunshot wounds during a battle in Perak, where he continued to lead his team under the revolutionary slogan, "Agi Idup Agi Ngelaban" (As long as I live, I shall fight).

Statistically, during the peak of the communist threat and the Indonesian Confrontation phase, non-Malay communities made up an estimated 60% of the membership of the 1st Reconnaissance Regiment deployed in domestic operations and United Nations peacekeeping missions in the Congo.
Furthermore, between the 1960s and the late 1970s, non-Malay personnel comprised around 30% of the entire armed forces workforce, with higher representation recorded in the navy and air force.
Historical records estimate that more than 500 soldiers and 1,300 police officers lost their lives during the Emergency.

Apart from the physical military aspects, psychological warfare in the country was also pioneered by a non-Muslim intelligence expert, Too Chee Chew. As the head of the psychological warfare section of the Federation of Malaya from 1956 to 1983, he utilised a deep understanding of the Malayan Communist Party's (MCP) doctrines and ideologies to formulate counter-propaganda strategies through leaflets and radio broadcasts, which effectively prompted thousands of communist guerrillas to surrender.

His capacity as the chief adviser to Tunku Abdul Rahman during the Baling Talks (1955) proved critical in analysing Chin Peng's diplomatic manoeuvres, thereby protecting the nation's sovereignty from the implications of an unfavourable agreement. His sacrifice was immense, given that this role made him a prime target for assassination by the enemy throughout nearly three decades of service.
Economic and social development

In terms of economic development and physical capital formation, early-generation labourers and entrepreneurs from the Chinese and Indian communities were primary drivers of Malaya's extractive sector and basic infrastructure. Their involvement in the tin mining and rubber plantation industries positioned Malaya as a leading global commodity producer.

The surplus capital generated from these sectors funded the construction of the country's earliest public amenities, including educational institutions, hospitals, and modern transportation networks like the road and railway systems.

In the modern era, equity ownership and strategic investments from the non-Muslim corporate sector continue to contribute to gross domestic product (GDP) growth and large-scale job creation. According to data from the statistics department, the non-Muslim demographic constitutes around 30% to 35% of the total citizen population driving the domestic market.

These corporate contributions are balanced by structured corporate social responsibility initiatives based on universal welfare. Corporate giants founded by non-Muslim entrepreneurs channel substantial financial contributions annually through charitable foundations – such as the YTL Foundation, Hong Leong Foundation, and Ananda Krishnan/Usaha Tegas — for academic scholarships and post-disaster humanitarian aid regardless of ethnicity or religious belief.

Additionally, human capital in both the public and private professional sectors is heavily supported by the involvement of the non-Muslim community in medicine, law, the judiciary, higher education, as well as technical and civil service corps, ensuring the continuity of the country's bureaucratic operations.
Sports

In the international sports arena, the contributions of non-Muslim athletes serve as instruments of public diplomacy and national integration. World-class sports legends such as Lee Chong Wei (badminton), Nicol David (squash), Pandelela Rinong (diving), R. Arumugam (football), and M Jegathesan (athletics) have demonstrated high commitment to raising the country’s sporting reputation globally.

The majority of Malaysia's early Olympic medals were contributed by non-Muslim athletes, including three silver medals by Chong Wei (2008, 2012, 2016) as well as the historic achievement of Pandelela as the country's first female athlete to win an Olympic medal (bronze in 2012 and silver in 2016).
Diversity

The diversity of art, culture, and heritage brought by the non-Muslim community has enriched Malaysia’s pluralistic identity on the international stage. The integration of traditional dances, musical expressions, traditional attire, architectural designs, and unique local gastronomy not only strengthens the tourism sector but also shapes a dynamic national cultural ecosystem.

Interfaith human connections are also manifested through inclusive social phenomena, such as the case of Chee Hoi Lan, who raised a Muslim foster child in strict compliance with Islamic practices. Such social narratives prove that national integration and the spirit of racial camaraderie are fundamental elements that must be preserved to guarantee geopolitical stability and the long-term prosperity of the nation.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8abf3bff1da3daba: Mujurlah Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi tidak hadir pada majlis perasmian muktamar PAS semalam. Saya kata 'mujur' kerana jika beliau hadir beliau akan dengar ucapan dasar Presiden PAS Hadi Awang secara langsung. Loud and clear.

Mungkin Zahid akan merasa 'disakiti'. Jika tidak sakit hati mungkin terkejut dan terperanjat kerana apa yang dilaungkan Hadi itu dilakukan ketika PAS sedang ghairah mahu jalin kerjasama dengan Umno, berlatarkan electoral pact yang berjaya di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan tempoh hari.

Lazimnya ucapan dasar presiden mana-mana parti politik akan disediakan awal dengan dibantu think tank masing-masing. Memanglah ucapan dasar presiden untuk ahli parti, but in this case pada hemat saya Hadi dan PAS ada nawaitu mahu sampaikan mesej direct ke muka Zahid. Ini kerana Hadi yakin Zahid akan hadir.

Presiden Umno dijangka hadir apabila PAS menghulurkan undangan. Saya kira Zahid sudah beri confirmation akan hadir. Jika tidak masakan Setiausaha Agung PAS Takiyuddin Hassan memberitahu muktamar kehadiran Zahid yang dinanti-nantikan terpaksa dibatalkan "pada saat akhir kerana urusan yang tidak dapat dielakkan".

Mungkinkah Zahid sudah menghidu atau dapat info apa yang akan diucapkan Hadi? Wallahualam. Apa pun Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki si setiausaha agung Umno hadir mewakili Zahid. Tak tahulah saya sama ada berdesing telinga beliau mendengar ucapan Hadi.

At least this part of the Hadi speech: "Setiap kerusi Dewan Undangan Negeri dan Parlimen yang telah dimenangi pada PRU 15 wajib dipertahankan". Perhatikan istilah yang Hadi gunakan yakni 'wajib'. Bukan 'seharusnya' atau 'perlu' tetapi 'wajib' maka PAS akan bertanding di semua kerusi yang disandang. No two ways about it.

Kata Hadi lagi: "Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah dan Perlis (SG4) sebagai 'negeri pangkalan' mesti terus dikekalkan penguasaannya, diperkukuh pentadbiran serta dilaksana agenda Islam mengikut bidang kuasa negeri."
That does not leave much for Umno-BN jika kerjasama dengan PAS dijalin. Sebenarnya sehari sebelum ucapan Hadi, mood 'PAS menguasai semua' sudah dirasai pada muktamar Pemuda PAS.

Umpamanya Ketua Pemuda PAS Kedah Ilyas Ahmad dipetik berkata usaha menyatukan umat Islam di peringkat persekutuan perlu dipimpin oleh PAS dan PAS juga tidak seharusnya lagi memberi laluan calon perdana menteri kepada parti lain. That is as clear as it can get. Beberapa perwakilan muktamar juga bercakap apa yang PAS mesti buat jika menang PRU16.

Kata Ketua Penyelidik Ilham Centre Yusri Ibrahim menerusi catatan di Facebook, penegasan PAS akan membuka episod baru dalam kebarangkalian kerjasama Umno-PAS menuju PRU16. Beliau ambil Terengganu sebagai contoh, "Jika PAS bertegas, hanya ada satu kerusi Parlimen dan lima kerusi DUN berbaki untuk ditandingi oleh Umno jika kerjasama dimeterai. Tetapi semua kerusi tersebut disandang oleh Bersatu."
Maka kata Yusri, "sudah tentu Wawasan akan bermatian menuntut dan mempertahankan kerusi tersebut kerana kepada Wawasan merekalah pewaris pusaka Bersatu dalam Perikatan Nasional."
"Jika kerusi tersebut dibahagi sama rata, Umno Terengganu berpotensi bertanding sekitar tiga kerusi sahaja dalam PRU16 nanti. Inilah scenario awal yang boleh difahami."
Itu belum lagi kita bercakap mengenai kerusi Parlimen dan DUN negeri-negeri lain.

Dalam pada itu, penganalisis James Chin dari Universiti Tasmania semalam dipetik FMT berkata Umno tampak cuba melemahkan perdana menteri meskipun berikrar menyokong Anwar Ibrahim sehingga tamat penggal Parlimen.

"Mereka mengenakan tekanan kerana tidak mahu hilang momentum (setelah menang PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan bersama PN serta confident menang PRN Melaka kelak). Adakah Anwar akan tunduk? Saya rasa masih awal untuk bercakap mengenainya. Anwar juga sedang mengatur perikatan baharu tanpa Umno," kata Chin.
Chin menjangkakan hubungan PH-BN akan semakin buruk sambil Umno terus berdolak dalik. Saya setuju dan tidak mungkin Anwar dan PH tidak perasan.

Berikutan ucapan Hadi semalam, Umno tertekan. Jika usul wajib berkait kerjasama dengan Umno diterima sebelum muktamar ditangguhkan hari ini, Umno tertekan juga tetapi saya tidak pasti adakah ia relevan memandangkan apa yang diucapkan Hadi yang saya sebut tadi.

Amat menarik apa agaknya reaksi Perhimpunan Agung Umno terhadap perkembangan di muktamar PAS. PAU akan berlangsung minggu depan yakni 9 hingga 12 September. Menarik juga kerana kepimpinan tertinggi PAS diundang ke upacara perasmian. Adakah Hadi akan hadir? Iya, kata Asyraf.

Menutup penulisan ini saya ulang apa yang pernah dinyatakan pada artikel terdahulu iaitu Umno sedang buat apa yang ia tuduh PAS buat dulu sehingga terkuburnya Muafakat Nasional. Apa yang PAS buat waktu itu? Bermain dua kolam, kata Umno. PAS berbaik dengan Umno dan pada masa sama berbaik-baik dengan Bersatu, musuh ketat Umno.
Sekarang Umno berbaik-baik dengan PH di peringkat persekutuan dan berbaik-baik dengan PAS di peringkat negeri sambil menyerang PH. Ertinya Umno main dua kolam.
Bagi saya sudah sudahlah main dua kolam. You can't have your cake and eat it too. Itu kata omputih. Orang Melayu kata simple je: "jangan nak makan kelilinglah".

The government’s plan to fast-track the e-commerce bill and consider registration requirements for platforms is timely.

E-commerce platforms are not neutral connectors between sellers and consumers; they are complex ecosystems built on heavy investments, extracting rental income from locked-in consumers and dependent businesses.
While platforms appear “free” to users, sellers pay steep costs—search ads, commissions, vouchers, and shipping campaigns—to remain visible.
Through network effects, data concentration, and control over transactions, platforms dictate how businesses access markets and reach consumers.

Their power and decision-making effectively make them private regulators, governing both businesses and consumers. Dependence on algorithmic profiling, automated decisions, and predictive analytics deepens the imbalance of power.
A recent fundamental research grant study by Universiti Malaya’s law faculty identified several major harms in Malaysia’s e-commerce sector:
Market access, data dependency
Platforms set operational rules—visibility rankings, traffic, fees, and data insights.

Meanwhile, businesses build reputation and rankings over time, but this visibility is tied to platform data, which cannot be replicated elsewhere. Non-transferability locks sellers in, strengthening platform dominance and widening the power gap.
Price, advertising pressures

By leveraging data and AI analytics, platforms fuel intense price and advertising competition. This forces businesses into trade-offs between cost efficiency and product quality, undermining long-term consumer welfare.
Predatory pricing

Platforms often sell below cost, subsidising vouchers and shipping to drive weaker competitors out. Exclusive contracts with affiliated businesses further distort competition, as transaction revenues fall below logistics and fulfilment costs.
Self-preferencing

Platforms use internal data to identify successful third-party products, replicate them under private labels, and manipulate search algorithms to favour their own offerings. This sidelines independent sellers.
Algorithmic bias
Search and recommendation systems are coded to favour certain products or brands, undermining neutrality and fairness.
Data asymmetry
Platforms aggregate granular transaction and consumer behaviour data from sellers, using it to optimise proprietary retail strategies, leaving sellers disadvantaged.
Algorithmic repricing
Automated pricing tools trigger margin wars, forcing smaller sellers into unsustainable profit thresholds.
Fee exploitation
Locked-in businesses face rising fees, mandatory ad spending, and high fulfilment costs simply to maintain visibility.
Vertical restraints
Platforms enforce price-parity clauses, mandatory discounts, and algorithmic penalties, stripping sellers of pricing flexibility and eliminating competition.
Exclusive dealing

Platforms restrict sellers to list exclusively on their marketplace (“single-homing”), penalising cross-listing. Though competition law limits exclusivity to two years, platforms’ shorter contracts often auto-renew, cumulatively foreclosing competition and reducing consumer choice.
Tied logistics

Platforms increasingly force sellers to use their own logistics services, sidelining independent delivery companies and raising costs for businesses with existing systems. Consumers lose delivery options, while competition in logistics is destroyed.
Unfair Contracts

“Take-it-or-leave-it” contracts impose restrictive clauses on both businesses and consumers. Price-parity rules prevent sellers from offering cheaper prices elsewhere, while sudden changes in platform terms expose both sides to exploitation. Consumer protection laws are weakened as liability is shifted away from platforms.
Cross-border factory dumping

Certain platforms integrate directly with Chinese manufacturers via proprietary software, dictating production in real time. This model bypasses import taxes through loopholes, flooding markets with cheap, unsafe products. Platforms cannot claim neutrality when they control supply chains, data, and algorithms.
Copying and grooming

Platforms mine seller dashboards to identify successful local products, replicate them through white-label factories, and push replicas to the top of feeds. Local merchants often find their intellectual property registered abroad, undermining expansion efforts.
International precedents

Global regulators are acting against platform abuses. In the US case of Oberdorf v. Amazon (2019), Amazon was held liable as a “seller” for defective third-party products, recognising its active role in sales and distribution.
In Europe, the Digital Services Act (2022) imposed record fines on AliExpress (Euros €550m) and Temu (€200m) for failing to curb illegal and unsafe goods.

Closer to home, Thailand introduced strict platform regulations in 2022, the Philippines enacted the Internet Transactions Act (2023), Vietnam suspended Temu and Shein for registration non-compliance before passing its Law on E-Commerce (2025), and Indonesia banned Temu to protect local industries.
Conclusion
Malaysia’s upcoming e-commerce bill must directly address structural algorithmic, competitive, and consumer harms.
Platforms are not neutral intermediaries but powerful private regulators shaping markets, data flows, and consumer access.
Without robust legal boundaries, Malaysia risks undermining trust in e-commerce, harming consumers, and weakening domestic retail and manufacturing sectors.
